strengths: Provides a unified DINO-informed design that is instantiated in two distinct SLAM paradigms (NeRF-based tri-plane and 3DGS-based), showing that a single Scene Structure Encoder (SSE) can be plugged into both implicit and explicit neural representations. This dual-pipeline demonstration is more than most single-backbone SLAM papers offer.

Evaluation is broad and multi-faceted: three standard benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM), tracking metrics (ATE RMSE), reconstruction metrics (accuracy, completion, completion rate, depth L1), and rendering metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS), plus memory/FPS analysis in Table 6. The generalization study (Table 4) applying SSE to six existing encodings (Co-SLAM, ESLAM, PLGSLAM, SNI-SLAM, Point-SLAM, MonoGS, SplaTAM, SGS-SLAM) is a genuinely useful piece of evidence about the portability of the idea.

Ablations are reasonably well designed: Table 5 separates the contribution of raw DINO features, EDINO features from the SSE, and global bundle adjustment, and Table 4 isolates the effect of adding DINO to existing backbones while holding the rest of the pipeline fixed. This is the right style of evidence for the claim being made.

The 3DGS pipeline shows a substantial tracking improvement on TUM (avg ATE 1.36 cm vs. 2.83/3.27/3.73 for MonoGS/SplaTAM/GS-SLAM), which is the strongest single result in the paper and suggests the approach has real practical value in at least one regime.
The architecture figures (Figs. 2-4) are informative, the losses are stated explicitly, and loss weights, resolutions, keyframe thresholds, and hardware are reported, which supports reproducibility.

The paper correctly identifies a real gap: most NeRF/3DGS SLAM systems optimize only pixel-wise color/depth and do not exploit higher-level self-supervised features, and it shows this supervision can be added without semantic labels or predefined categories.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The core idea, adding dense pretrained/self-supervised feature supervision to neural SLAM, is closely related to existing feature- or semantics-supervised SLAM (e.g., NICE-SLAM feature grids, SNI-SLAM semantic features, which the paper itself compares against). The SSE is essentially an MLP + cross-attention refinement block, and the paper does not include the control experiment that would establish that DINO specifically matters: no comparison against other frozen backbones (CLIP, ImageNet-supervised, or even random features) or against simply adding more optimization capacity. Without that, it is unclear whether the gains come from DINO's structure or from extra dense supervision/loss terms.

Several claims are overstated relative to the numbers. The abstract/intro assert state-of-the-art performance on Replica/ScanNet/TUM, but on Replica the NeRF pipeline is clearly worse than Point-SLAM on accuracy (1.94 vs. 1.41 cm) and depth L1 (0.66 vs. 0.44 cm), and only ties on completion rate; on ScanNet its average ATE (7.1) is essentially tied with Point-SLAM (7.1) and only marginally better than ESLAM/PLGSLAM (7.4). For the 3DGS pipeline, SSIM (0.971) is below Gaussian-SLAM (0.993), so 'state-of-the-art rendering' is not uniformly supported.

The ablation evidence for the 'crucial' role of DINO in the 3DGS pipeline is weak on the rendering side: in Table 5 (lower), removing DINO changes PSNR 21.43 -> 21.50, SSIM 0.78 -> 0.79, LPIPS 0.39 -> 0.39. Only depth RMSE shows a meaningful gap (12.67 -> 9.55), and that could plausibly be an artifact of adding an extra feature-consistency loss rather than of DINO's semantic content.

Fairness/comparability of the large 3DGS tracking margin (1.36 cm vs. 2.8-3.7 cm on TUM) is not established. The paper does not state whether baselines were re-tuned under the same protocol, whether the same keyframe selection/co-visibility strategy was used for all methods, or whether the DINO feature loss is used at all in the 3DGS tracking thread (the text says tracking optimizes only color and depth residuals, so the tracking benefit is indirect and unanalyzed). A result of this magnitude normally needs explicit protocol controls.

No limitations, failure-mode, or societal-impact discussion. There is no analysis of when DINO features hurt or fail (dynamic scenes, severe motion blur, cross-domain/outdoor data), no discussion of the cost of the frozen ViT, and no acknowledgment that the 3DGS pipeline runs at 0.61 FPS, which is far from the 'real-time' framing used in the introduction.

Minor presentation and consistency issues: PSNR scales differ drastically across tables (39 on Replica vs. 21.5 on ScanNet) without an explanation in the caption, and Table 5's caption/rows mix NeRF-Replica and 3DGS-ScanNet settings in a way that invites misreading. The 'Comp.rate' and 'Comp.' columns and the dagger-marked entries need clearer description of the post-processing protocol.

strengths: The paper proposes a well-motivated framework (DINO-SLAM) that leverages self-supervised DINO features as higher-level scene understanding cues for dense RGB-D SLAM, avoiding the need for semantic annotations, pre-defined categories, or offline training—an appealing property for practical deployment.

The Scene Structure Encoder (SSE) is a sensible design that refines DINO features with geometric (depth) and appearance information through cross-attention (Eqs. 2–3), producing enhanced DINO (EDINO) features that encode part-whole and inter-component relationships.

The paper demonstrates broad applicability by instantiating the same SSE design across two distinct neural representation paradigms (NeRF-based and 3DGS-based SLAM) and by integrating it into multiple existing encodings (hash-grid, tri-planes, neural points, 3DGS) in Table 4, which strengthens the generality claim.

Evaluation is comprehensive, spanning three standard benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM) with a full suite of mapping/tracking/rendering metrics, plus component ablations (Table 5) that isolate the contributions of DINO features, EDINO features, and global BA.

Competitive quantitative results: DINO-SLAM achieves the best completion (1.64 cm), completion rate (97.06%), and RMSE (0.51 cm) on Replica among NeRF-based methods, best PSNR/LPIPS/RMSE among 3DGS methods on Replica, and the best average ATE on ScanNet (3DGS) and TUM (both pipelines), with favorable memory/FPS in Table 6.
The presentation is generally clear, with informative figures (Figs. 2–4) that map each loss and supervision signal to a concrete component, and the contributions are explicitly stated.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate and somewhat incremental: the central idea—injecting foundation-model/self-supervised features into dense SLAM—overlaps substantially with prior feature/semantic-augmented SLAM (e.g., SNI-SLAM, which the paper cites), and the SSE is essentially a cross-attention refinement module. The paper does not convincingly delineate what is fundamentally new beyond combining DINO features with NeRF/3DGS SLAM.

State-of-the-art claims are somewhat overstated. On Replica (Table 1), Point-SLAM achieves clearly better Accuracy (1.41 vs 1.94 cm) and Depth L1 (0.44 vs 0.66 cm), and Gaussian-SLAM achieves better SSIM (0.993 vs 0.971); on ScanNet (Table 2), DINO-SLAM (NeRF) ties PLGSLAM at 7.1 ATE. The abstract/intro claim of “superior performance … compared to state-of-the-art methods” should be qualified.

Some reported gains are marginal and plausibly within noise: 3DGS PSNR 39.12 vs MonoGS 38.94 (+0.18 dB), and RMSE 0.30 vs 0.31/0.32. No variance/seed analysis is provided to support significance of these small differences.

The 3DGS baseline set is limited (SplaTAM, Gaussian-SLAM, MonoGS, GS-SLAM) and does not include more recent or directly comparable DINO/semantic-augmented 3DGS SLAM systems; similarly, the closest related work (SNI-SLAM) is discussed but not benchmarked on the same protocols.

Methodological details are thin in places: Eq. (10) does not actually show how EDINO features are injected into the Gaussian parameters (despite the text claiming a “modified Gaussian equation”), and the dimension/alignment between per-Gaussian feature embeddings and the rendered feature map is unclear, affecting reproducibility.

Table 6 FPS/memory appear to reflect the encoder/decoder footprint rather than end-to-end SLAM throughput; no end-to-end runtime or convergence-time comparison is given, which is important given the additional cross-attention overhead.

The loss weighting (5.0 for encoding, 0.01 for DINO feature) is provided without sensitivity analysis, and the paper does not analyze failure cases (e.g., dynamic scenes, poorly textured environments) or discuss limitations of relying on DINO features.

The paper claims not to require semantic labels, but it does not compare against semantic-feature SLAM baselines on equal footing to substantiate the advantage of DINO over semantic cues; Table 4 uses semantic masks (*) only on some baselines, which may not be a fully fair comparison.

strengths: Unified design: a single Scene Structure Encoder and feature-level supervision scheme is instantiated in both a NeRF-style (tri-plane) pipeline and a 3DGS pipeline, which is a reasonable demonstration of generality across neural representations.

Generality evidence is reasonably strong: Table 4 shows that adding the proposed DINO/EDINO supervision improves four different backbones (hash-grid, tri-planes, neural points, 3DGS) on Replica, suggesting the idea is not tied to one representation.

Broad empirical study: three standard benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM), both tracking (ATE RMSE) and reconstruction/rendering metrics, plus component ablations (DINO vs EDINO vs bundle adjustment) and a cost table (size/FPS).

Tracking results on ScanNet and TUM are the most convincing part of the paper (e.g., ScanNet ATE 7.1 vs 8.7 for Co-SLAM/ESLAM and 9.5 vs 15.2 for MonoGS; TUM 1.36 vs 1.50 for GS-SLAM), and the NeRF variant attains the best completion (1.64), completion rate (97.06) and RMSE (0.51) on Replica.
The method avoids semantic labels, pre-defined categories and offline training, which is a genuine practical advantage over semantic SLAM pipelines.
Implementation details such as loss weights, tri-plane resolutions, keyframe selection criteria and bundle-adjustment strategy are partially reported, which helps reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. Supervising neural SLAM with features from a pretrained self-supervised/semantic network has been explored before (e.g., SNI-SLAM with semantic features, and the authors' own related work notes that WildGS-SLAM already uses DINO features for uncertainty). The actual delta here is 'use DINO instead of semantic features' plus an attention-based fusion module, and the claim of being the first to bring DINO cues into SLAM is not well supported by the cited literature. DINOv2, which is the standard choice for dense correspondence, is never considered or compared against DINOv1 ViT-S.

The gains on the primary benchmark do not clearly support the central claim. On Replica with 3DGS, PSNR 39.12 vs MonoGS 38.94, LPIPS 0.062 vs 0.070, RMSE 0.30 vs 0.32 are within noise, and SSIM 0.971 is substantially below Gaussian-SLAM's 0.993. The statement that DINO-SLAM achieves 'state-of-the-art performance in both rendering quality and tracking accuracy among all 3DGS-based methods' is therefore not supported by the authors' own table.

Internal inconsistency between ablation and narrative. Table 5 shows that removing DINO features changes 3DGS rendering from PSNR 21.50 to 21.43 and SSIM 0.79 to 0.78, i.e. essentially nothing, yet the text claims 'substantial performance degradation across mapping, rendering, and tracking metrics'. The ablation evidence for the rendering claim (a core selling point of the paper) is missing.

Overclaiming in the abstract/introduction. The blanket statement that DINO-SLAM 'achieve[s] superior performance on the Replica, ScanNet, and TUM compared to state-of-the-art methods' is contradicted by the tables: on Replica the NeRF pipeline is clearly worse than Point-SLAM in accuracy (1.94 vs 1.41) and depth L1 (0.66 vs 0.44). The claims should be scoped to the metrics where the method actually wins.

Missing and poorly handled baselines. The most directly comparable family - semantic/feature-supervised neural SLAM (SNI-SLAM, SGS-SLAM, NEDS-SLAM, Hier-SLAM) - is absent from the main comparison tables, even though the paper's thesis is precisely that higher-level features help. SNI-SLAM appears only in an ablation with the footnote 'uses ground-truth semantic masks', and it has no entry in the reference list, which is an attribution problem. Fairness of the reproduced baselines (tuning, identical keyframe/culling protocols) is also not documented.

Method specification is too loose for reproduction. In Eqs. (2)-(3) the geometric and appearance features f_g and f_a have different dimensions yet are multiplied directly (f_g f_d^T), the scaling uses d_a inconsistently, and the query/key/value roles and the spatial extent over which attention is applied are never defined. The dimensionality of the DINO/EDINO features embedded in each Gaussian parameter is not reported, and it is not explained how patch-level DINO features (stride 8/16) are reconciled with per-pixel rendering/feature losses.

Cost reporting is hard to believe and under-analyzed. Table 6 lists Ours (3DGS) at 27.8 MB, smaller than MonoGS (28.5 MB), despite adding an extra feature channel per Gaussian; the paper does not state whether this is encoder/decoder-only memory or total memory, nor the runtime cost of extracting DINO features per frame. Both pipelines run at ~0.6 FPS, and the additional feature-extraction overhead is never quantified.

Loss weighting is inconsistent across the two pipelines (DINO-feature loss weight 1.0 for 3DGS vs 0.01 for NeRF, encoding feature loss 5.0) with no justification or sensitivity analysis, which makes it hard to judge how much tuning was needed to obtain the reported numbers.

Presentation issues: Figures 2 and 4 are extremely dense and difficult to parse, several symbols (beta, d_a, z_n, the superscript indices in Eq. 12) are undefined or ambiguous, and the 'dagger' footnote refers to meshes but is applied to metric tables. No limitations, failure cases, or societal-impact discussion is provided.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: the paper convincingly argues that vanilla DINO features lack 3D geometric understanding and proposes a geometry-aware lifting (SGE) to remedy this. The ablation in Table 2 (A/B/B'/C and D/E/F) directly supports this claim, showing that geoDINO features roughly double the gains of vanilla DINO and outperform naive depth concatenation, which is a meaningful and non-trivial empirical finding.

Broad generality demonstrated through extensive integration: the SGE is injected into a wide variety of scene encodings (hash-grids, tri-planes, neural points, 3DGS, 2DGS) in Table 1, showing consistent improvements. This is one of the strongest aspects of the paper and directly supports the 'design paradigm' framing.

Strong and comprehensive empirical evaluation across three standard benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM) covering both tracking (ATE RMSE) and mapping/rendering metrics. The GS variant achieves state-of-the-art rendering and tracking on Replica (Table 3), and both variants achieve best average ATE on TUM (Table 6).

Responsible engineering analysis: Tables 7 and 8 provide memory/FPS/runtime breakdowns showing the SGE overhead is negligible in most cases, and Table 4 evaluates robustness to depth noise—two aspects often missing in SLAM papers.
The paper is clearly written, with informative figures (Fig. 2, 3, 4, 5) that make the two pipelines understandable, and honest discussion of where baselines (e.g., PLGSLAM on ScanNet) still excel.
weaknesses: Moderate technical novelty: the core SGE module is essentially a depth-guided cross-attention over DINO features (Eqs. 2–3), and feature-level supervision with a frozen foundation model is a fairly standard recipe. The integration of DINO into SLAM has already been explored (e.g., SNI-SLAM, Go-SLAM, SNI-SLAM-style semantic SLAM), so the contribution is more of a well-executed design study than a fundamentally new method.

Not uniformly state-of-the-art: on ScanNet (Table 5) the NeRF variant (6.9) is slightly worse than PLGSLAM (6.8) and worse than Point-SLAM on several sequences, and on Replica accuracy the NeRF variant (1.88) is worse than Point-SLAM (1.41). The paper acknowledges this but the 'superior performance' claims in the abstract are somewhat overstated relative to the tables.

The GS pipeline appears to inherit much of its design (keyframe strategy, BA, loss formulation) from GauS-SLAM; the contribution in this pipeline is largely the addition of per-Gaussian geoDINO feature channels and a DINO-feature loss, which limits the perceived depth of the GS-side contribution.

Fairness of baseline comparison is not fully established: several entries are marked '†' as obtained directly from authors, and it is unclear whether all baselines were retrained under identical protocols (same frames, same keyframe strategy, same number of optimization steps). This matters because the reported gains over GauS-SLAM on Replica (e.g., 41.42 vs 40.25 PSNR) are modest.

Limitations and failure modes are barely discussed: the conclusion only briefly mentions future extensions (loop closure, sub-mapping) but does not analyze scenarios where the method degrades (e.g., textureless regions, dynamic scenes, or depth-sensor failure modes beyond the Gaussian noise test). A dedicated limitations section would strengthen the paper.
The depth L1 improvements in Table 4 for the noisy-depth condition are large but only tested on one scene (office1); the robustness claim would be stronger with multi-scene evaluation.

strengths: Broad and well-demonstrated applicability: the Scene Geometry Encoder (SGE) is injected into five+ distinct scene encodings (hash-grids, tri-planes, neural points, 3DGS, 2DGS) and yields consistent improvements in Table 1, which is exactly the kind of plug-in generality the paper claims. This makes the contribution more than a single-system paper.

The ablation in Table 2 is well designed and directly supports the central scientific claim: vanilla DINO features give only marginal gains (B/E), naive depth concatenation (B') is limited, while geoDINO features produce roughly double the improvement (C/F). This cleanly isolates the value of the proposed geometry-aware lifting over a naive alternative.

Strong empirical results across three standard benchmarks. The GS variant reaches state-of-the-art on Replica for rendering quality and tracking (Table 3: 41.42 PSNR, 0.994 SSIM, 0.021 LPIPS, 0.05 cm RMSE), and the NeRF variant obtains the best completion/completion-rate/RMSE. Competitive results on ScanNet (Table 5) and TUM (Table 6) round out the evidence.

The depth-noise robustness experiment (Table 4) is a nice, honest addition: DINO-SLAM (GS) trained on noise-corrupted depth still outperforms GauS-SLAM with clean depth, providing evidence that the SGE is not merely overfitting to perfect depth.

Efficiency is reported rather than hidden: memory usage, FPS, and a detailed computational breakdown of the SGE overhead are given (Tables 7 and 8), including the fact that the GS variant adds negligible cost over GauS-SLAM.

The manuscript is clearly written, with an informative pipeline figure (Fig. 2), a readable SGE architecture diagram (Fig. 3), and good integration of qualitative reconstruction/rendering comparisons (Fig. 6). Related work coverage is appropriate and the positioning relative to existing DINO-in-SLAM works is discussed.
weaknesses: Moderate technical novelty relative to the framing. The SGE is essentially a two-stage cross-attention module that injects depth-derived features into frozen DINOv2 features, and the paper itself acknowledges prior integration of DINO features into SLAM (SNI-SLAM [62], Go-SLAM [37], SGS-SLAM [61], Loss-SLAM [40]). Describing the two pipelines as "two foundational paradigms" overstates what is largely the same feature-level loss applied within two existing backbones (ESLAM, GauS-SLAM). The main gains come from adding a feature-prediction head plus feature loss, a technique already common in NeRF/SLAM literature.

The feature-supervision design is under-analyzed and potentially degenerate. In the NeRF pipeline, L_gf directly regresses the tri-plane encoding τ_D toward the high-dimensional geoDINO features with an L1 loss (Eq. 6), rather than supervising a rendered quantity. It is not discussed why this is preferable, nor whether this admits trivial solutions (e.g., feature collapse to a constant map, or per-view memorization of DINO features extracted from the current frame). No diagnostics (feature variance, PCA/feature-map visualizations over training, collapse checks) are provided. For the GS pipeline, the mechanics of how the per-Gaussian geoDINO channel is initialized, optimized and whether it influences geometry versus only appearance are also thinly specified.

The method is restricted to RGB-D input, since the geometry signal in the SGE is depth. This excludes the large monocular SLAM portion of the field, and the limitation is neither stated in the abstract/introduction nor discussed in a limitations section; the generality claims are therefore broader than the actual scope.

Efficiency trade-off is understated in the claims. The NeRF variant nearly halves FPS relative to ESLAM (2.55 vs 4.62 on Replica room0, Table 7). This is reported in the table but the abstract and introduction emphasize "superior performance" without flagging the cost. Additionally, Table 8's whole-sequence times (3510 s vs 3387 s) appear inconsistent in magnitude with the per-frame SGE overhead and with the reported FPS drop, which needs reconciliation.

Evaluation reporting could be tightened. (a) The protocol for metrics such as completion rate (97.22) and depth L1 (0.63 cm) versus numbers in the original baseline papers is asserted to be identical but not reconciled; the mesh culling of [49] and any differences in mesh extraction/post-processing should be explicitly described. (b) Results on ScanNet and TUM are averages over few sequences with no variance or significance testing, and several per-sequence entries are worse than baselines (e.g., ScanNet 0000, 0181 in Table 5). (c) Scalability beyond memory measurements is not demonstrated; no large-scale/outdoor scenes. (d) The absence of loop closure and sub-mapping, acknowledged only as future work, means comparisons against methods with global BA (e.g., PLGSLAM, which wins on ScanNet) are not fully controlled.

No discussion of failure modes, limitations, or societal impact. For a method whose performance depends on the reliability of frozen DINOv2 features and on depth quality, an analysis of when the approach breaks down (texture-less regions, dynamic scenes, extremely noisy or missing depth) would materially strengthen the paper.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and well-motivated problem: injecting self-supervised foundation-model (DINO) features into dense RGB-D SLAM. The idea of lifting DINO features with depth to obtain geometry-aware (geoDINO) features is sensible and the framing around combining semantic priors with 3D geometry is reasonable.

Broad empirical validation of the core 'generality' claim: Table 1 shows that the proposed SGE module can be plugged into very different backbones (hash-grids, tri-planes, neural points, 3DGS, 2DGS) and yields consistent improvements, and the comparison against SNI-SLAM (which already uses DINO features for segmentation) supports the argument that naive DINO features are insufficient.

The component ablation (Table 2) is informative: it isolates vanilla DINO, simple DINO+depth concatenation, and the full geoDINO, and shows geoDINO is responsible for most of the gain, in both NeRF- and GS-based pipelines. This directly supports the central claim of the paper.

The GS-based variant achieves state-of-the-art results on the Replica benchmark across rendering and tracking metrics, and the paper includes useful system-level analyses (memory and runtime in Tables 7-8) and a depth-noise robustness study (Table 4), which strengthens the practical assessment.
The manuscript is generally readable, with clear pipeline figures (Figs. 2-5) that communicate the NeRF- and GS-based designs.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty relative to the framing. The Scene Geometry Encoder is essentially a two-stage cross-attention module over DINO and depth features, and the overall contribution is feature-level supervision/embedding applied to existing SLAM pipelines. Calling these 'two foundational paradigms' overstates the conceptual advance.

Consequential reproducibility gaps in the method. The geoDINO loss L_gf = ||tau_D - f_gD||_1 is defined between a 3D tri-plane feature field and a 2D per-pixel feature map, but the paper never specifies how the correspondence is established (which 3D points are sampled, whether they are unprojected with depth, how per-ray ambiguity is resolved) or how dimensionalities match. Similarly, for the GS pipeline it is never explained how a per-Gaussian geoDINO feature is 'assigned' or parameterized (dimension, storage, compression), which makes the reported memory (343 MB in Table 7) difficult to reconcile with a 384-dim DINO feature per Gaussian.

Some results are overclaimed. The NeRF variant is not state-of-the-art on accuracy or depth L1 on Replica (Point-SLAM is better on both), yet the abstract and introduction claim 'superior performance' and 'state-of-the-art accuracy'. Several improvements are marginal (e.g., RMSE 0.06 -> 0.05 on Replica GS; small deltas in Table 1), and no multiple-seed runs or variance estimates are reported, so some gains may be within run-to-run noise.

Runtime overhead for the primary NeRF pipeline is substantial: Table 7/8 report ESLAM dropping from 4.62 to 2.55 FPS (~45% slowdown) for DINO-SLAM (NeRF), which is far from 'negligible' and should have been discussed as a practical limitation rather than downplayed.

There is an unaddressed circular dependency: the SGE consumes the depth map (which in SLAM is itself estimated by the system) to produce features that supervise the scene representation, which then refines depth. The implications of this feedback loop, especially under inaccurate depth, are not analyzed beyond a single-scene noise study (office1).

Minor but real technical inconsistencies: Eq. (9) describes a spherical Gaussian with radius r, which contradicts the anisotropic covariance formulation stated just above; the attention equations (2)-(3) are unusual (queries/keys swapped relative to the description, and attention weights applied to f_D rather than to values) and not well motivated.

Robustness and failure-case analysis is thin: the depth-noise experiment covers only one scene, and there is no discussion of degenerate cases (textureless regions, dynamic objects) that are central to SLAM.
